## What this code does

This repository contains OpenSCAD code for printing multi-line name badges.  Up
to four lines of text are supported.  For less than four lines, leave the lines
which are not being used blank and the code will adjust automatically.  

There is no need to edit the .scad file directly.  All the relevant parameters
can be configured within OpenSCAD using the OpenSCAD Customizer (Ensure
`Customizer`) is ticked in the `Windows` menu, and this is the recommended way
of designing badges.

## Features

* Badges of any printable size
* Up to 8 SVG format single colour images per badge
* 1 - 4 lines of text - each line can be configured independently
* Use any font installed on the system in any font size
* Indenting of text for fine control of formatting and flowing around images
* font styles (bold, italic etc.)
* Horizontal scaling to ensure badge text fits on the line
* Up to 8 colours (including background)
* Option for cutout/debossed foreground for a 3d effect / single colour printing
* Embossed (3D) text also supported
* Left, right, centre align
* Fine tune vertical alignment of each line
* Lanyard style and magnetic attached badges
* Optional border around the edge of the badge
* Square/rectangular and circular/oval badge shapes
* Custom badge shape from using any vector SVG file as a silhouette
* Rectangular badges have rounded corners by default
* Create multiple similar badges from a .CSV file (using the supplied convertor)
* Radial text on circular arcs (particularly good for round badges)

## Programs

| Name                     | Purpose                                            |
| :----------------------: | :------------------------------------------------- |
| name_badges.scad         | Program used to generate badges - load in OpenSCAD |
| import_csv_badge_data.py | Script to convert .csv badge data to OpenSCAD JSON |
| svg_pos_calculator.ods   | Spreadsheet to calculate position data for images  |
| example_name_badges.json | Some example configurations                        |

## Prerequisites

A 3d printer is required.  The badges can be printing on a single colour printer
with the letters in negative relief (set the default colour to "cutout") but
this is probably not very visible unless the lowered sections are then painted,
so a multi-colour 3d printer is strongly recommended.

A [nightly build](https://openscad.org/downloads.html#snapshots) of OpenSCAD is
necessary to build the files for printing. Parameters are adjustable from
within the configurator to allow your preferred size. The `manifold` renderer
should be used (`"Edit" -> "Preferences" -> "Advanced"`).  The `text-metrics`,
`import-function`, `predictable-output`  and `lazy-union` features should also
be turned on (`"Edit" -> "Preferences" -> "Features"`).

I recommend turning off automatic previewing, and always doing a full render, as
this seems to actually be quicker than previewing.  I have experienced program
crashes when previewing which do not occur when running a full render.

Appropriate slicer software for your 3d printer is also required.  I use
[OrcaSlicer](https://orcaslicer.com/).

## Badge styles

Five badge styles are available:

magnetic
: single sided with a rectangular cutout in the back to allow the self adhesive
metal strip of a magnetic attachment to sit flush with the badge surface

lanyard
: double sided with a hole in the top centre of the badge to attach a lanyard

hanging
: A double sided badge with a protruding hole in the top centre of the badge, in
the style of a christmas ornament or drop earring

plain-1sided
: single sided badge, no cutout or lanyard hole

plain-2sided
: double sided badge, no cutout or lanyard-hole

Note that a double sided badge must be thicker than the depth of the text.

## Formatting tips

* The badge images are placed in the order that they are listed.  Later images
  always "cover" images under them.  The badge text may overlap the images and
  will be printed on top of them.
* The text and image layers are slightly offset.  This is because OpenSCAD does
  not cope well with aligning them if they are flat surfaces.  In practice these
  very small (< 0.1 mm of height) differences will be optimised away by the
  slicer, but they still appear slightly offset when viewed in OpenSCAD or the
  slicer.  This is perfectly normal and nothing to worry about.
* Overlapping badge text is not supported.  If there is a requirement for text
  to overlap other text, or to have more than 4 text items on the badge, to use
  non-horizontal text, or to have an image placed on top of text, the best way
  to accomplish this is to create the text as an SVG image in a program like
  Inkscape and import it as an image.
* If horizontal scaling is disabled, or a non rectangular badge is used, text
  may flow over the side of the badge.  Setting the `disable-text-clipping`
  parameter to `false` will prevent this, but is disabled by default as it has
  caused some instability in OpenSCAD.
* It can be hard to get vector image files to line up correctly.  The
  spreadsheet `svg_pos_calculator.ods` (in OpenDocument format, but Excel will
  also open it), can be used to calculate the necessary scale and position
  values to get everything to line up on the badge surface.  The position and
  size values for the original SVG files can be read using Inkscape and put
  into the spreadsheet.
* The program interprets an empty line of text as meaning there is no more text
  data.  If, for example, there is a requirement to create a badge with text on
  lines one and three but not on line two is required, put a " " (space)
  character on line two. Otherwise only the first line will be added to the
  badge.
* If using embossed images, put the lowest images first.  Lower images will not
  in general overwrite higher ones

## Creating multiple badges

The script allows the user to design a single badge by hand, but this can be
laborious when creating multiple badges of the same design.

A Python helper script `import_csv_badge_data.py` is available to create
multiple badges at once.  Put badge data into per badge per row, 1 column per
line (this script does no automatic wrapping) then run and save this data as a
comma separated value (CSV) file in the same directory as the `name_badges.scad`
file. Then run the following command.

```
python import_csv_badge_data.py -i <.csv file> -o <.json file>
```

The JSON file can then be read into OpenSCAD by adding it to the 
`Multiple Badges` section of the Customizer.  A test file `authors.csv` is
provided to try this out with.  Those feeling particularly brave, can
use the -s option to write data in CSV format directly from standard input.

## Radial text on badges

Enable this by setting a non-zero radius for a text line.  Standard badge
position parameters are ignored when this mode is active.

Often rather than text which goes all the way around the badge, what will be
desired is for text on the bottom line to flow anti-clockwise and clockwise on
the top.  The name badge generator tries to be smart about this and by
default generates anti-clockwise text for text lines with a centre between 120
deg and 240 deg.  This is configurable in the "radial text" settings (or can
just be avoided entirely by setting an angle above 360 degrees).

By default circular text going almost all the way around the circle and centred
at the top of the badge will be generated, but this can be configured to suit
the user.

A sensible default text size for your text will be picked, but it is only a
guess, and can result in text the wrong size, as well as different sized text
on different badges depending on the length of the message.  Automatic text
sizing can be turned off for more control.  Letters which go beyond the 
length of the assigned arc will not be printed.

Radial text queries the font metrics to calculate character spacing, which
seems to use a lot of data storage and may give a "normalised tree is growing
past xxxx elements" error.  The only fix for this is to increase the number of
elements handled by the model.  Some attempt has been made to optimise the code
to reduce these errors, but they still persist.

## How to print the badges

The easiest way to import the generated badge into a slicer is to to export it
from OpenSCAD as a .3mf file and load that into the slicer directly.  It can
also be imported into an existing project. In OrcaSlicer this is done by using
the `import` button in the top left of the main panel, or using the `Add Models`
option from the context menu.  

For either method in OrcaSlicer, see below for a detailed workflow, as
OrcaSlicer can be picky about the order in which the steps need to be done, but
in essence the process is to change the colours of each filament by selecting
the parts individually in `objects` mode.  The colours can be set to anything
for which filament is available - there is no restricting to the colours
provided in OpenSCAD, which are picked arbitrarily for having good contrast.

If the .3mf files do not work with a particular slicer, it is also possible to
generate individual .stl files for each separate colour using the colour
selection box in the Customizer and combined together in the slicer. In Orca
Slicer select `Add models` then select both colour files, and allow the slicer
to combine them into a single object. Then use `objects` mode to set the colour
of the filaments.

## Importing and colouring .3mf files in Orca Slicer

When generating multiple badges, it is recommended to use multiple objects per
colour for ease of reuse, and where the final print will not fit on one plate.

### Single badge or multiple badges with single object per colour

1) Right click on plate and select `Add Models`
2) Select the file to be imported
3) Select `import geometry` when prompted
4) When asked whether to import as a single object with multiple parts select
   `yes`
5) Switch to the `objects` view and change the filament colours so that the
   object looks right

### Multiple badges with multiple objects per colour

1) Right click on plate and select `Add Models`
2) Select the file to be imported
3) Select `import geometry` when prompted
4) When asked whether to import as a single object with multiple parts select
   `no` - note that this may cause Orca Slicer to display warnings until the
   process is complete.
5) Switch to the `objects` view
6) There will now be long list of models.  These will be in order, so 
   - for a 3 colour design,
     - models 1, 4, 7. 10 ... will be one colour
     - models 2, 5, 8, 11 ... another 
     - models 3, 6, 9, 12 ... the third
   - For a 4 colour design 
     - Colour 1: Models 1,5,9,13 ...
     - Colour 2: Models 2,6,10,14 ...
     - Colour 3: Models 3,7,11,15 ...
     - Colour 4: Models 4,8,12,16 ...
7) Select all of the models of the same colour using CtrL+Left click on the
   model name, then set them all to the desired colour.  Repeat for each colour
   in turn.
8) There should now be a number of groups of colours, starting at the bottom,
   select the same number as the number of colours in the badge, so 3 for a 3
   colour model, 4 for a 4 colour model etc.  Right click and select `Assemble`
   to combine these into a single object.
9) Repeat until all the badges are together
10) It should now be possible to use auto-arrange to fit all your badges onto a
    plate.

## Printing tips

 - Make sure that the first layer prints slowly for crisp images.  A quarter
   speed seems to work well (I use `first layer` 12.5, `first layer infill` 27,
   `initial layer travel speed`: 50%, with 2 slow layers.
 - For best results, set the print order for the first layer so that the outer
   edge of complex shapes is printed first, which will guide the filament into
   the right places.  In OrcaSlicer this is done using the `plate options` for 
   each plate.
 - in OrcaSlicer, always use the `Arachne` wall generator and `Precise Wall`
   option, and set the minimum wall widths lower if printing a design with fine
   detail.  `Small area flow compensation` is also recommended.
 - Reducing line width can also be helpful with fine detail, but can also lead
   to prints not sticking to the base, and does not generally make much
   difference unless printing fine detail.
 - Cheap hairspray can be helpful if problems with sticking are experienced.
 - If print lines are visible on the surface of the badge, reducing the bottom
   surface wall flow ratio (to about 0.8 or so) can sometimes help with getting
   a cleaner print.
 - Increasing elephants foot compensation to 0.4 seems to improve quality somewhat
 - Setting wall printing order to "outer/inner" can help produce crisper images - 
   since the badges have no overhangs, there is likely no downside to this

## Example badges

Some sample OpenSCAD configurations are provided in the
`example_name_badges.scad` file.  

 - To use these easily, just rename the file to `name_badges.scad`.  (This is
   not done by default to avoid overwriting personal configurations).  
 - The 
   [Cat Silhouette.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_silhouette.svg) 
   file referred to can be downloaded from Wikimedia Commons.  
 - The fonts used can be downloaded from Google Fonts if they are not installed 
   on the local system
   - [Orbitron](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Orbitron)
   - [IM Fell English](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/IM+Fell+English)
   - [Macondo](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Macondo)
 - Use `import_csv_badge_data.py` to create the `authors.json` file

This project is based on a GitLab [Project Template](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/gitlab-basics/create-project.html).

Improvements can be proposed in the [original project](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/project-templates/rails).

### CI/CD with Auto DevOps

This template is compatible with [Auto DevOps](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/topics/autodevops/).

If Auto DevOps is not already enabled for this project, you can [turn it on](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/topics/autodevops/#enabling-auto-devops) in the project settings.

### Developing with Gitpod

This template has a fully-automated dev setup for [Gitpod](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/integration/gitpod.html).

If you open this project in Gitpod, you'll get all dependencies pre-installed and Rails server will open a web preview.

The model was originally developed for inert volcanic particles (tephra) and has a track record of 50+ publications on different model applications and code validation, as well as an ever-growing community of users worldwide, including academia, private, research, and several institutions tasked with operational forecast of volcanic ash clouds. ## BadgeVMS SDK

This is the C API for writing BadgeVMS applications.

Using the C SDK requires you have installed a working RISC-V toolchain. One easy way to do is by [installing ESP-IDF](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/get-started/index.html).

Check the `examples/` folder for example projects.

### Setup

for now we just symlink `include` to `firmware.git/include`.

```
$ git clone badgevms_sdk.git
$ git clone firmware.git
$ cd badgevms_sdk
$ ln -s ../firmware/include include
$ export BADGEVMS_SDK=$(pwd)
$ cd examples
$ make clean && make
```

### Running an example

Using the loader functionality in firmware it's easy to quickly test your compiled (example) apps using `loader_client` from this repository. The Makefile template includes an `upload` target that invokes this utility. The `loader_client` depends on some python libraries though, so make sure to set up a virtual env or similar.

venv setup:

```
$ cd tools && python3 -m venv venv && . ./venv/bin/activate
$ pip install -r requirements.txt
```

upload:

```
$ cd examples/input_basic && make
$ make upload SERIALPORT=/dev/ttyUSBX_or_whatever
```

# BadgeMaker

Make badges, get happy, win prizes*

\*you may not win prizes.

## Description

Badgemaker is a project to hopefully reduce the amount of work it takes to make a badge for a convention. Started to reduce the amount of work it takes to create around 15,000 badges the long term goal is instead to create a versitile and modular system that allows for the inclusion of all sorts of additional information such as qr codes, identifiers, names, custom titles, logos etc.

Open source because the only way the world gets better is if we all chip in, and this can reduce the amount of work for an average con staffer to create cool badges.

## Getting started

Badgemaker is written entirely in python to make it easy to port between operating systems. It should be as easy as download, create a venv (or don't. I'm not your mom.) and then install the dependencies with pip.

## Usage

The intended use for badgemaker is to provide customizable templates that can be then used to mass produce badges.

First, customize `badgemaker.conf.tpt` to fit an event. the eventID is an identifier that should be unique to that event, such as a custom ID number, or other information important to the run of badgemaker for an event.

The current badge template is provided within the `badge_template.tmp` file located in the badge_templates directory. This should be customized for each badge type that's intended to be created.

Once these have been created, badges can be provided in a properly formatted file with one badge per line, and badges will be created in groups of 500 for a PDF.

500 is an arbitrary number that was chosen because the PDF library borb appears to choke on anything higher. If I can figure out how to remove the reliance on borb, or how to remove this limit, I'd like to output all badges of one type (or possibly all types) in one PDF.

# BadgerDB

[![Go Reference](https://pkg.go.dev/badge/github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4.svg)](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4)
[![Go Report Card](https://goreportcard.com/badge/github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4)](https://goreportcard.com/report/github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4)
[![Sourcegraph](https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/dgraph-io/badger/-/badge.svg)](https://sourcegraph.com/github.com/dgraph-io/badger?badge)
[![ci-badger-tests](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger/actions/workflows/ci-badger-tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger/actions/workflows/ci-badger-tests.yml)
[![ci-badger-bank-tests](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger/actions/workflows/ci-badger-bank-tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger/actions/workflows/ci-badger-bank-tests.yml)
[![ci-badger-bank-tests-nightly](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger/actions/workflows/ci-badger-bank-tests-nightly.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger/actions/workflows/ci-badger-bank-tests-nightly.yml)

![Badger mascot](images/diggy-shadow.png)

BadgerDB is an embeddable, persistent and fast key-value (KV) database written in pure Go. It is the
underlying database for [Dgraph](https://github.com/dgraph-io/dgraph), a fast, distributed graph
database. It's meant to be a performant alternative to non-Go-based key-value stores like RocksDB.

## Project Status

Badger is stable and is being used to serve data sets worth hundreds of terabytes. Badger supports
concurrent ACID transactions with serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) guarantees. A Jepsen-style
bank test runs nightly for 8h, with `--race` flag and ensures the maintenance of transactional
guarantees. Badger has also been tested to work with filesystem level anomalies, to ensure
persistence and consistency. Badger is being used by a number of projects which includes Dgraph,
Jaeger Tracing, UsenetExpress, and many more.

The list of projects using Badger can be found [here](#projects-using-badger).

Please consult the [Changelog] for more detailed information on releases.

Note: Badger is built with go 1.23 and we refrain from bumping this version to minimize downstream
effects of those using Badger in applications built with older versions of Go.

[Changelog]: https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

## Table of Contents

- [BadgerDB](#badgerdb)
  - [Project Status](#project-status)
  - [Table of Contents](#table-of-contents)
  - [Getting Started](#getting-started)
    - [Installing](#installing)
      - [Installing Badger Command Line Tool](#installing-badger-command-line-tool)
      - [Choosing a version](#choosing-a-version)
  - [Badger Documentation](#badger-documentation)
  - [Resources](#resources)
    - [Blog Posts](#blog-posts)
  - [Design](#design)
    - [Comparisons](#comparisons)
    - [Benchmarks](#benchmarks)
  - [Projects Using Badger](#projects-using-badger)
  - [Contributing](#contributing)
  - [Contact](#contact)

## Getting Started

### Installing

To start using Badger, install Go 1.23 or above. Badger v3 and above needs go modules. From your
project, run the following command

```sh
go get github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4
```

This will retrieve the library.

#### Installing Badger Command Line Tool

Badger provides a CLI tool which can perform certain operations like offline backup/restore. To
install the Badger CLI, retrieve the repository and checkout the desired version. Then run

```sh
cd badger
go install .
```

This will install the badger command line utility into your $GOBIN path.

## Badger Documentation

Badger Documentation is available at [https://badger.dgraph.io](https://badger.dgraph.io)

## Resources

### Blog Posts

1. [Introducing Badger: A fast key-value store written natively in Go](https://hypermode.com/blog/badger/)
2. [Make Badger crash resilient with ALICE](https://hypermode.com/blog/alice/)
3. [Badger vs LMDB vs BoltDB: Benchmarking key-value databases in Go](https://hypermode.com/blog/badger-lmdb-boltdb/)
4. [Concurrent ACID Transactions in Badger](https://hypermode.com/blog/badger-txn/)

## Design

Badger was written with these design goals in mind:

- Write a key-value database in pure Go.
- Use latest research to build the fastest KV database for data sets spanning terabytes.
- Optimize for SSDs.

Badger’s design is based on a paper titled _[WiscKey: Separating Keys from Values in SSD-conscious
Storage][wisckey]_.

[wisckey]: https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/fast16/fast16-papers-lu.pdf

### Comparisons

| Feature                       | Badger                                     | RocksDB                       | BoltDB    |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | --------- |
| Design                        | LSM tree with value log                    | LSM tree only                 | B+ tree   |
| High Read throughput          | Yes                                        | No                            | Yes       |
| High Write throughput         | Yes                                        | Yes                           | No        |
| Designed for SSDs             | Yes (with latest research <sup>1</sup>)    | Not specifically <sup>2</sup> | No        |
| Embeddable                    | Yes                                        | Yes                           | Yes       |
| Sorted KV access              | Yes                                        | Yes                           | Yes       |
| Pure Go (no Cgo)              | Yes                                        | No                            | Yes       |
| Transactions                  | Yes, ACID, concurrent with SSI<sup>3</sup> | Yes (but non-ACID)            | Yes, ACID |
| Snapshots                     | Yes                                        | Yes                           | Yes       |
| TTL support                   | Yes                                        | Yes                           | No        |
| 3D access (key-value-version) | Yes<sup>4</sup>                            | No                            | No        |

<sup>1</sup> The [WISCKEY paper][wisckey] (on which Badger is based) saw big wins with separating
values from keys, significantly reducing the write amplification compared to a typical LSM tree.

<sup>2</sup> RocksDB is an SSD optimized version of LevelDB, which was designed specifically for
rotating disks. As such RocksDB's design isn't aimed at SSDs.

<sup>3</sup> SSI: Serializable Snapshot Isolation. For more details, see the blog post
[Concurrent ACID Transactions in Badger](https://hypermode.com/blog/badger-txn/)

<sup>4</sup> Badger provides direct access to value versions via its Iterator API. Users can also
specify how many versions to keep per key via Options.

### Benchmarks

We have run comprehensive benchmarks against RocksDB, Bolt and LMDB. The benchmarking code, and the
detailed logs for the benchmarks can be found in the [badger-bench] repo. More explanation,
including graphs can be found the blog posts (linked above).

[badger-bench]: https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger-bench

## Projects Using Badger

Below is a list of known projects that use Badger:

- [Dgraph](https://github.com/dgraph-io/dgraph) - Distributed graph database.
- [Jaeger](https://github.com/jaegertracing/jaeger) - Distributed tracing platform.
- [go-ipfs](https://github.com/ipfs/go-ipfs) - Go client for the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS),
  a new hypermedia distribution protocol.
- [Riot](https://github.com/go-ego/riot) - An open-source, distributed search engine.
- [emitter](https://github.com/emitter-io/emitter) - Scalable, low latency, distributed pub/sub
  broker with message storage, uses MQTT, gossip and badger.
- [OctoSQL](https://github.com/cube2222/octosql) - Query tool that allows you to join, analyse and
  transform data from multiple databases using SQL.
- [Dkron](https://dkron.io/) - Distributed, fault tolerant job scheduling system.
- [smallstep/certificates](https://github.com/smallstep/certificates) - Step-ca is an online
  certificate authority for secure, automated certificate management.
- [Sandglass](https://github.com/celrenheit/sandglass) - distributed, horizontally scalable,
  persistent, time sorted message queue.
- [TalariaDB](https://github.com/grab/talaria) - Grab's Distributed, low latency time-series
  database.
- [Sloop](https://github.com/salesforce/sloop) - Salesforce's Kubernetes History Visualization
  Project.
- [Usenet Express](https://usenetexpress.com/) - Serving over 300TB of data with Badger.
- [gorush](https://github.com/appleboy/gorush) - A push notification server written in Go.
- [0-stor](https://github.com/zero-os/0-stor) - Single device object store.
- [Dispatch Protocol](https://github.com/dispatchlabs/disgo) - Blockchain protocol for distributed
  application data analytics.
- [GarageMQ](https://github.com/valinurovam/garagemq) - AMQP server written in Go.
- [RedixDB](https://alash3al.github.io/redix/) - A real-time persistent key-value store with the
  same redis protocol.
- [BBVA](https://github.com/BBVA/raft-badger) - Raft backend implementation using BadgerDB for
  Hashicorp raft.
- [Fantom](https://github.com/Fantom-foundation/go-lachesis) - aBFT Consensus platform for
  distributed applications.
- [decred](https://github.com/decred/dcrdata) - An open, progressive, and self-funding
  cryptocurrency with a system of community-based governance integrated into its blockchain.
- [OpenNetSys](https://github.com/opennetsys/c3-go) - Create useful dApps in any software language.
- [HoneyTrap](https://github.com/honeytrap/honeytrap) - An extensible and opensource system for
  running, monitoring and managing honeypots.
- [Insolar](https://github.com/insolar/insolar) - Enterprise-ready blockchain platform.
- [IoTeX](https://github.com/iotexproject/iotex-core) - The next generation of the decentralized
  network for IoT powered by scalability- and privacy-centric blockchains.
- [go-sessions](https://github.com/kataras/go-sessions) - The sessions manager for Go net/http and
  fasthttp.
- [Babble](https://github.com/mosaicnetworks/babble) - BFT Consensus platform for distributed
  applications.
- [Tormenta](https://github.com/jpincas/tormenta) - Embedded object-persistence layer / simple JSON
  database for Go projects.
- [BadgerHold](https://github.com/timshannon/badgerhold) - An embeddable NoSQL store for querying Go
  types built on Badger
- [Goblero](https://github.com/didil/goblero) - Pure Go embedded persistent job queue backed by

# badge-nfc-webhook

This is firmware for the NorthSec 2026 badge that turns it into an
NFC-driven webhook trigger. Tap a card on the back of the badge, the
badge fires an HTTP POST to a server you control, and the server does
whatever you've mapped to that card — play a song, unlock a door or
fire your home-automation scenes.

I use mine to start kid songs on my Sonos bar for now.

**disclaimer: this is vibecoded**

The hardware is an ESP32-S3-WROOM-1 with 16 MB of flash, an ST25R3916
NFC front-end, a 6-button D-pad, and an 18-pixel NeoPixel ring. None of
that needs to be true for you to read this README, but it's nice to
have context.

Everything you might want to change at runtime — Wi-Fi credentials,
webhook URL, brightness, the hours the badge is awake, the admin
password — lives behind a small web UI hosted on the badge itself.
You should rarely need to reflash once the badge is in your hands.

## Getting the badge running

The first time you boot a freshly flashed badge, it has no idea what
network to join. Rather than failing silently, it gives up after about
twenty seconds and brings up its own open Wi-Fi access point so you can
go talk to it.

1. Flash the firmware (`pio run -t upload` — see *Building* below).
2. After it boots, look for an open Wi-Fi network called
   `nsec2026-XXXX` (the four hex characters are the last bytes of the
   Wi-Fi MAC). Join it from your phone or laptop.
3. Most modern OSes pop a captive portal. If yours doesn't, open
   `http://192.168.4.1/` in a browser.
4. Fill in your Wi-Fi credentials, the URL of the webhook server, and
   anything else you want to change. Click *Save & reboot*.
5. The badge restarts, joins your real network, and prints its new IP
   on the serial console. From here on the same web UI lives at that
   IP — no need to dig around the badge again unless you change networks.

> remember now **.htacces -> admin:badge**

![Badge web UI in AP fallback mode](badge-ap-setup.png)

### Default Wi-Fi when nothing is configured

The badge has no factory-set Wi-Fi credentials. On the first boot
it Wi-Fi connection fails and falls back to AP mode within 20s.
The fallback access point is **open** (no password) and named after 
the badge's MAC `nsec2026-XXXX`. Once you save any SSID and reboot,
the badge stops broadcasting that AP and joins your network instead.

To reach the setup page after your Wi-Fi has changed, either:

- **Reboot** the badge. If the saved SSID is now unjoinable, the boot-time
  fallback opens the `nsec2026-XXXX` AP after 20s, or
- **Hold button B while the badge boots** (press and keep it held through
  power-on/reset). The badge skips the station attempt entirely and comes
  straight up in the open `nsec2026-XXXX` AP — this works even when the
  saved Wi-Fi is still reachable. Release B, connect, and reconfigure.

### Admin password once connected

The web UI is protected by HTTP Basic auth with the username `admin`
and a default password of `badge`. 

If you forget the password, plug into USB and run
`cfg set admin_pw newpw` + `cfg commit` at the serial.

## How the NFC → webhook part works

Each tag is identified by its UID ex: 
> 53EB36A4130001 for my Victor Timberlake

When you tap a card, the badge POSTs a small JSON to your server:

```
POST <webhook_url>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "uid":     "53EB36A4130001",
  "tech":    "NFC-A",
  "ndef_id": "card:42",      // text record, if any (NFC-A/T2T and NFC-V tags)
  "badge":   "nsec2026-XXXX"
}
```

The badge posts to the exact URL you configure If you're using the
bundled `php-nfc` or `nginx-nfc` server, the setting 
(e.g. `http://192.168.0.42:8082/nfc`).

When the request completes, the LED ring flashes once so you can
see what happened:

| Flash colour | What it means                                                       |
|--------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Green        | Server returned `2xx`. Whatever you mapped actually fired.          |
| Yellow       | Server returned `4xx`. The badge reached it, but it refused — most often the UID has no mapping yet, or you've pointed `webhook_url` at the wrong path. |
| Red          | `5xx`, timeout, DNS failure, or refused connection. The badge couldn't get a usable response at all. Check Wi-Fi, the server is up, and the URL is reachable from the badge's IP. |

The same outcome lands in the live-log panel of the web UI as
`webhook: POST … -> NNN` (or `failed: …`), so you can correlate the
colour with a status code if you need more detail than a glance.

> **Heads up — leaving a tag on the antenna.** The badge fires the
> webhook *once per tap* (edge-triggered: it watches for the field to
> go quiet before it'll re-fire for the same UID). However, the
> ST25R3916 wake-up mode auto-averages its baseline over time, so a
> card that *never* leaves the reader eventually gets re-classified
> as "new" and replays — typically about every 10 minutes. If you
> don't want the replay, take the card off when you're done with it.
> Or make a stand where the NFC reader is vertical.

## The badge's buttons

The D-pad and the two action buttons do a few different things:

| Button | What it does                                |
|--------|---------------------------------------------|
| UP     | Cycle to the next LED pattern               |
| DOWN   | Turn the LEDs off                           |
| LEFT   | Dim by 10 %                                 |
| RIGHT  | Brighter by 10 %                            |
| A      | LED sweep (one direction)                   |
| B      | LED sweep (other way). Also: **hold at boot** to force Wi-Fi setup (AP) mode |

## The time gate

The badge is battery-powered. To make a 1000 mAh LiPo last most of a
day you want to do less work when nobody's around.

By default the badge syncs the time via NTP after it joins Wi-Fi, then
shuts down the Wi-Fi radio and the NFC RF field between 23:00 and 07:00
local time. You can change the hours, the timezone, or disable the gate
entirely (set on and off to the same value) from the web UI.

Rough power numbers, for sanity:

| What's running                              | Avg draw | Runtime |
|---------------------------------------------|----------|---------|
| LEDs off, NFC + Wi-Fi active                | ~25 mA   | ~40 h   |
| LEDs on (mid brightness), gate active       | ~80 mA   | ~10 h   |
| Time gate has shut everything down          | ~5 mA    | days    |

If the badge has never gotten time from NTP yet, it assumes it's
inside the active window and starts polling normally. So a fresh
power-on at 3 AM still works — you just won't get the battery savings.

## Configuration: where settings come from

Settings fall through a small priority chain:

1. **Web UI** — the easy path. Persisted to NVS. Survives reboots.
2. **Serial** — `cfg set <key> <value>` then `cfg commit`. Useful
   when Wi-Fi is broken and you can't reach the UI.

The web UI has *Factory reset* if you want to wipe NVS and start over.

## Turning the web UI off

The web UI is on by default, if you'd rather lock the badge down
after deploying it permanently somewhere, there's a 
*Keep this web UI enabled* the settings. Uncheck it, save-reboot. 
The badge boots without starting its HTTP server at all.

You can only re-enable it from the serial (`cfg set web_enabled 1`, 
then `cfg commit`).

## Updating the firmware over Wi-Fi (OTA)

Once the badge is on your network, you don't need a USB cable to push
a new build. Open the setup page, scroll to **Firmware update**, pick
the new `firmware.bin`, and click *Upload & reboot*. Takes about 20s.
The badge restarts into the new image automatically.

### "I just want to try this firmware" — no build, no toolchain

If you don't want to install PlatformIO and you only need the binary,
grab the latest prebuilt bundle from the project's Releases page
(`badge-nfc-webhook-YYYYMMDD-SHA.zip`). It contains three files —
`bootloader.bin`, `partition-table.bin`, `firmware.bin` — and a short
README pointing back to the commands below.

You need exactly one tool — `esptool.py` — which is a single Python
package:

```bash
# macOS / Linux
python3 -m pip install --user esptool
# Windows
py -m pip install esptool
```

Then plug the badge in over USB and run:

```bash
esptool.py --chip esp32s3 erase_flash
esptool.py --chip esp32s3 --baud 460800 write_flash \
    0x0000   bootloader.bin \
    0x8000   partition-table.bin \
    0x20000  firmware.bin
```

Pick the right serial device with `--port /dev/cu.usbmodem101` (macOS)
or `--port /dev/ttyACM0` (Linux) or `--port COM5` (Windows) if esptool
doesn't auto-detect.

After the badge comes up, follow *Getting the badge running* above to
join the AP and configure it.

### Cutting a release (for the maintainer)

The repo ships a `.gitlab-ci.yml` that does this automatically. Tag a
commit with `vX.Y.Z` (anything matching `v\d…`) and push the tag:

```bash
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
```

GitLab builds the firmware, packages it via `scripts/make-release.sh`,
publishes a Release tied to the tag, and attaches three asset links:
the `.zip` bundle, the `.tar.gz` bundle, and a direct `firmware.bin`
download for OTA.

To build a bundle manually without CI:

```bash
pio run
scripts/make-release.sh
```

## The serial console

The badge always has a working serial on its USB-Serial-JTAG port,
at 115200 baud. It's there for when you've misconfigured Wi-Fi and
the web UI is unreachable, and for debugging.

```bash
pio device monitor
```

Once at the `badge>` prompt:

```
cfg show                  list every stored setting
cfg set wifi_ssid Home    change a value (not yet persisted)
cfg commit                save it to NVS
cfg reboot                restart the badge
log set wifi debug        turn up the chattiness of one subsystem
log set * warn            back to the quiet default
ip                        print the badge's current IP
reboot                    restart the badge
```

Settings you can `cfg set`: `wifi_ssid`, `wifi_pass`, `webhook_url`,
`dedupe_ms`, `gate_enabled`, `gate_start`, `gate_end`, `tz`,
`admin_pw`, `web_enabled`. Passwords are masked in `cfg show`. The
badge's ID (derived from its MAC) is read-only.

The web UI's right column shows the same log stream the serial console
does, with a 4 KB ring buffer.

## Tooling — what to install before building

You only need PlatformIO. It downloads and manages ESP-IDF v5.2.1
for you, so you don't need to touch anything else.

- macOS / Linux: `python3 -m pip install platformio`, then either
  put `~/.local/bin` on your `PATH` or invoke `pio` from there.
- Windows: install Python 3.10, then `py -m pip install platformio`.

### Required for the host

- **Python 3.10** (PlatformIO).

### Quick "is everything wired up" check

```bash
python3 --version
pio --version
```

If those lines work and the cable shows the badge as a serial device,
you're ready to build.

## Building

```bash
pio run                                  # just build
pio run -t upload                        # build + flash
pio device monitor                       # watch the serial output
```

## What lives where

```
badge-nfc-webhook/
├── CMakeLists.txt          top-level project
├── platformio.ini          PlatformIO wrapper
├── sdkconfig.defaults      build defaults
├── partitions/badge.csv    flash layout (3 MB factory slot for the app)
├── main/                   entry point + Kconfig
├── components/             one folder per subsystem
│   ├── config_store        NVS-backed config + serial REPL commands
│   ├── wifi_provision      STA connect with AP-fallback
│   ├── setup_web           HTTP server + setup page + log buffer
│   ├── nfc_reader          ST25R3916 driver glue (rfal-based)
│   ├── webhook_client      esp_http_client POST + queue
│   ├── button_input        debounced 6-button watcher
│   ├── led_indicator       NeoPixel ring driver
│   ├── time_gate           NTP-backed wake/sleep window
│   ├── rfal/               vendored ST RF abstraction layer
│   └── st25r3916/          vendored chip driver (polled IRQ)
├── boards/Nsec2026.json    PlatformIO board definition
├── scripts/                tiny flash / monitor wrappers
└── server/                 optional server that maps NFC UIDs to webhooks
    ├── php-nfc/            PHP resolver + admin UI + docker-compose
    └── nginx-nfc/          pure-nginx alternative (no edit UI)
```

The two vendored components (`rfal/`, `st25r3916/`) come from ST's
X-CUBE-NFC6 source; I've left a clearly-marked patches in
`st25r3916_irq.c` so the driver works without a hardware IRQ line (the
2026 badge doesn't wire one to the MCU). If you ever update the
upstream sources, those patches will need to be reapplied.
https://www.st.com/en/embedded-software/x-cube-nfc6.html

## The webhook server (optional)

The badge talks to whatever HTTP server you point it at — you can
write your own, or use one of the two reference implementations in
`server/`. Both speak the same `POST /nfc` shape described above.

- **`php-nfc/`** is a single-file PHP front-controller backed by a
  JSON map, with a small browser admin UI at the same URL for
  editing the mapping. POST or GET per card. Recommended.
- **`nginx-nfc/`** is the same idea, but as a vanilla nginx config —
  no runtime. The mapping lives in the config file   itself; to
  change it you edit the file and run `nginx -s reload`.

### Running php-nfc with docker compose

The easiest way to host `php-nfc` is the bundled `docker-compose.yml`:

```bash
cd server/php-nfc/
docker compose up -d
```

>UI: http://localhost:8082/

>Badge webhook URL: http://192.168.0.42:8082

A single php-cli container runs PHP's built-in HTTP server
(`php -S`) — no fastcgi, no nginx, no fpm. `mapping.json` and
`nfc.log` are stored in the same folder as the compose file and
persist across container restarts. To use a different host port,
change the `ports:` mapping in `docker-compose.yml`.

Why not put the URL on the card directly? I can just add a new card
without writing to a NFC tag.

## When things go wrong

The boot log on the serial console (or the live-log panel in the web
UI) is usually all you need.

- **No tags scan.** Look for `nfc:` lines. You should see
  `IC_IDENTITY = 0x2A` shortly after boot — that's the ST25R3916
  announcing itself. If it's `0xFF` or you see `not detected`, the chip
  is offline (loose ribbon, dead board).
- **Wi-Fi never associates.** The badge logs
  `STA_DISCONNECTED reason=N` on every retry. Reason 15 means the
  password is wrong; 201 means the SSID isn't visible (often 5 GHz —
  the ESP32-S3 only does 2.4 GHz).
